chapters.title: A map for the restless
chapters.src: The AP Framework, introduction and Part I
lines: The AP Framework is a summary of the philosophy of Acharya Prashant, an Indian teacher of Vedanta.
It covers seven questions: what is real, how we know, what liberation is, what has value, what the mind is, what a human being is, and what art is.
But it does not ask you to believe anything.
It calls itself a set of diagnostic tools: ways of catching a mistake while you are making it.
And the mistake it is looking for has a name: the ego.

chapters.title: The ache that returns
lines: Start with something everyone knows: dissatisfaction.
We change jobs, cities, partners and plans, and after a while the old ache comes back.
The framework says this ache is structural, not circumstantial. It is not about where you are.
So the real question is not whether we are trying hard enough.
It is whether the whole direction of our effort is wrong.

chapters.title: I am X
chapters.src: Section IV: the ego and its origins
lines: The ego, in this framework, is simply the felt sense of I am X.
Its roots are physical. The skin marks where the body ends and the world begins, and a separate, bounded self grows from that line.
A bounded self feels incomplete, so it reaches out and takes things in: my house, my country, my degrees, even my wounds.
Every possession, title and grievance makes it heavier. The framework calls this ego fattening.
The opposite, ego thinning, is a slow loss of that weight and self-concern.
It never reaches zero while the body lives. Some ego always remains; the framework calls it the ego floor.

chapters.title: The innocent machine
chapters.src: Sections IV and VI: ego, body and mind
lines: The ego also uses the body. Try reading a difficult book that threatens your opinions, and notice how quickly you feel sleepy.
That drowsiness is not just tiredness. The ego is using the body to escape.
The mind, memory and intellect, is called an innocent machine. It does what it is told.
Only the ego has agency. It is the senior partner.
So when there is suffering, the framework says, blame the right party: not the mind, but the ego that is driving it.

chapters.title: Two directions
lines: All movement, the framework says, goes in one of two directions.
The horizontal is change: gaining, achieving, collecting. A shopkeeper expands his business. A student collects degrees. A pilgrim multiplies his penances.
Energy is spent and things change, but no height is gained. Everyone is moving on the same flat sheet.
The vertical is freedom. It is not about having more, but about the centre you act from becoming thinner.
The belief that enough horizontal effort will lift you vertically, the framework calls the biggest lie.

chapters.title: The engine and the empty tank
lines: Picture the ego as an engine. Desire is the fuel; action is the combustion.
The achiever's engine roars. He is always going somewhere.
The dropout has given up. His stillness looks like peace, but the tank has simply run out.
Refuel him with a new hope, and the old engine roars back.
Achiever and dropout stand on the same flat sheet. Losing desire is not the same as being free.

chapters.title: Seeing and intent
chapters.src: Sections IX and X: the formula for change
lines: So what does change? The framework gives a formula.
Seeing is honest observation of what is happening, before the ego adds its commentary and excuses.
Intent is the continuing choice to let the ego dissolve rather than protect it.
Neither works alone. Seeing without intent, it argues against Krishnamurti, changes nothing.
And intent is not willpower. Willpower fights an outside enemy, a habit or a craving, and leaves the ego in charge.
Intent turns against the ego's own wish to survive. That, the framework says, is the real battle.

chapters.title: The ledger and the frozen shoulder
chapters.src: Sections X and XV: the ledger, two kinds of freeze
lines: The ego also keeps a ledger: a running account of what it is owed. The gifts it gave, the hurts it suffered, the sacrifices it made.
While the ledger stays open, resentment has a purpose. The suffering is kept as proof of a claim.
Take a frozen shoulder. In one case the arm could move, but does not; the stiffness is a strategy, and the ledger stays open.
In the other, the joint is truly damaged, and exercise alone will not help.
Even then, one choice remains: to go and find a surgeon.

chapters.title: Two people, one song
chapters.src: Sections XI and XII: feelings and ethics
lines: Two people weep at the same piece of music. From outside, they look the same.
But for one, the ego is being confirmed and enlarged. For the other, it is being loosened. The direction is opposite.
Grief is like that too. Egoic grief mourns a lost possession; tenderness honours what helped dissolve the ego.
And joy, it says, can sit beside physical pain.
In ethics, mercy treats the symptom; compassion goes to the root.
The line of moral concern is sentience. An animal's suffering counts as much as a human's bodily pain.

chapters.title: Satyam, Shivam, Sundaram
chapters.src: Part I, axiology and aesthetics; Sections VIII and XVI
lines: The framework defines its highest values by what they are not.
Truth is what is not false. Beauty is what is not ugly. And Shiva, the auspicious, is whatever serves the ego's dissolution.
Satyam, Shivam, Sundaram: three names for one principle.
Great art, too, is made in the ego's absence. The artist disappears, and returns, and disappears again.
Creativity, it says, is creating without a creator.

chapters.title: Mirror and sun
lines: Because the ego is both contestant and referee, it cannot judge its own progress. An outside reference is needed: a teacher, a text, a tradition.
The teacher is like the sun, shining on everyone without bias. Who responds depends on who is ready to be disturbed.
The teacher is a mirror and a catalyst. He does not hand out liberation; he helps you see yourself more honestly.
Trust is given a little at a time, and withdrawn if it is not helping.
The relationship is complete when it is no longer needed, as with Krishna and Arjuna in the Gita.

chapters.title: Among the philosophers
lines: The framework sets itself against many traditions.
With Shankara's Advaita it shares the method of negation, but it rejects the witness, the sakshi, as the ego's last refuge.
With Nagarjuna it shares the method of negation, but it places the root of the problem in the body, not in thought.
Schopenhauer is its closest Western parallel. But Jung's individuation, it says, is the most sophisticated form of ego fattening, and the Stoic sage is an ego polished, not dissolved.
Neo-Advaita's claim that we are already enlightened is called the ego's cleverest evasion.
For the framework, enlightenment as a final state is impossible. Liberation is a direction: a journey without a destination.

chapters.title: The first superstition
chapters.src: Sections XIX and XX: the first superstition and conclusion
lines: Last, a warning for the rationalist, who questions religion, tradition and authority.
He questions everything, except the one who is questioning.

lines.q: The ego is the first superstition. It challenges everything, except itself.

lines: The framework's promise is modest. No faith, no technique, no renunciation; only honest self-observation.
Each time you catch the ego at work, it weakens, by a fraction.
And in that moment of catching, the one who was imprisoned is briefly absent. That, it says, is enough.
